hooks.text: NASA is currently shouting into a twenty-four-hour void.
Voyager 1 was never meant to leave our solar system.
Humanity's furthest probe is now sixteen billion miles away.

title: The Spacecraft One Light-Day Away From Earth
description: Voyager 1 is so far from Earth that its signals take nearly twenty-four hours to reach us. Discover how NASA keeps this interstellar traveler calling home.

beats.text: NASA is currently shouting into a twenty-four-hour void.
beats.visual: photograph of a Deep Space Network radio antenna dish pointing at the sky

beats.text: Most think our furthest spacecraft is still close to home.
beats.visual: diagram of the solar system showing planetary orbits and the sun, 2020

beats.text: But Voyager 1 actually crossed into interstellar space in 2012.
beats.visual: artist rendering of Voyager 1 crossing the heliopause into interstellar space, 2012

beats.text: It is now sixteen billion miles away from the sun.
beats.visual: technical diagram of the Voyager 1 spacecraft highlighting components

beats.text: NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory launched the probe back in 1977.
beats.visual: photograph of Titan III rocket launching Voyager 1 at Cape Canaveral, 1977
queries: Titan III rocket launch Cape Canaveral

beats.text: To keep it talking, engineers recently fired backup thrusters.
beats.visual: photograph of NASA engineers at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory control room

beats.text: These engines had slept unused for over thirty-seven years.
beats.visual: technical drawing of Voyager spacecraft propulsion thruster assembly

beats.text: It is now a lonely time capsule carrying our golden record.
beats.visual: photograph of the Voyager Golden Record cover, 1977

beats.text: Every radio message must cross that endless twenty-four-hour void.
beats.visual: artist concept of Voyager 1 drifting alone among distant stars
